# Exact critical cap covers and a maximum-volume variational problem

Assume d>=1. Let P be a finite set of integer points, let K_z be nonempty
compact convex fibers, and let S be their disjoint union above P. Write mu
for the sum of fiber d-volumes and M=mu(S)>0. Let

    beta=max_(y in S) inf_(closed ambient halfspaces H containing y) mu(H)/M.

The maximum exists by the same-fiber continuity and compactness argument in
`candidate a14cc5f809b2b766`.

The first result below assumes the already proved strict finite-cap-cover
lemma: for every epsilon>0 there are at most N nonvertical closed halfspaces,
each of mass less than (beta+epsilon)M, whose interiors cover S. In the
mixed-integer convex setting one can use N=2^n(d+1). This note proves that
the strict epsilon loss can be removed for a CLOSED cover.

## 1. Compactness of affine-threshold cap restrictions

Consider a sequence of nonvertical halfspaces. Divide its inequality by
the norm of its continuous component to write it as

    H_l={(z,x): u_l.x >= t_l(z)},    |u_l|=1,

where t_l is an affine function of z. On passing to a subsequence, u_l tends
to a unit vector u, and for every z in finite P the numbers t_l(z) tend in
the extended real line to t(z), which may be finite or infinite.

Define the limiting section inside R^d by

    L_z={x:u.x>=t(z)}       if t(z) is finite,
    L_z=empty              if t(z)=+infinity,
    L_z=R^d                if t(z)=-infinity.

For any fixed R<infinity, these sections on P x R B_d are realized by ONE
actual nonvertical ambient halfspace. Here is a proof that includes the
unbounded affine-coefficient case.

Write an affine function as w.(z,1), and let I be the subset of P with finite
limits. The vectors (t_l(z))_(z in I) lie in the image of the linear evaluation
map E_I:w -> (w.(z,1))_(z in I). This image is a closed linear subspace.
Hence there is w_0 with E_I w_0=(t(z))_(z in I).

Choose a linear right inverse J on im(E_I); it is bounded in finite dimension.
If w_l are the original affine coefficients, put

    v_l=w_l-w_0-J(E_I(w_l-w_0)).

Then E_I v_l=0, while the subtracted correction tends to zero. For every
z outside I, v_l.(z,1) therefore tends to the same signed infinity as t_l(z).
One sufficiently late v_l has ALL of these required strict signs
simultaneously. Fix that vector v. Taking a sufficiently large finite T makes
w=w_0+Tv agree with every finite t(z), exceed R at every +infinity coordinate,
and be less than -R at every -infinity coordinate. If I=P use w=w_0; if I is
empty the same proof uses the zero-dimensional evaluation map. Thus

    H={(z,x):u.x>=w.(z,1)}

has exactly the prescribed sections on P x R B_d.

For the original measure mu, whose fibers are bounded, mu(H_l) converges to
mu(H). At finite thresholds, the indicators converge except on the hyperplane
u.x=t(z), which has zero d-volume because u is nonzero. At infinite
thresholds they eventually converge everywhere on the bounded fiber to zero
or one. Dominated convergence on the finitely many fibers proves the claim.
This remains true for zero-volume fibers, which contribute nothing to mu.

There is also the following closed-graph property: if x belongs to a fixed
bounded fiber and belongs to H_l along a subsequence, then x belongs to L_z.
At a finite threshold this follows by taking limits in u_l.x>=t_l(z);
at +infinity eventual membership is impossible; at -infinity it is automatic.
The realizing halfspace H retains this membership inside the common ball.

## 2. A finite closed cover at the exact depth value

For epsilon_l tending to zero, take the assumed strict covers with at most
N caps. Pass to a subsequence with constant cardinality k<=N, and apply the
preceding compactification to each of the k cap sequences simultaneously.
Choose one common ball containing all original fibers. Let H_1,...,H_k be
the actual ambient halfspaces that realize all the limiting sections there.

Mass convergence gives

    mu(H_j) <= beta M        for every j.

They cover S. Indeed, fix any y in S. At each index l at least one of the k
caps contains y. One cap index contains y along an infinite subsequence.
The closed-graph property puts y in its limiting cap H_j. This is a direct
pointwise proof for EVERY y, including all zero-volume or boundary points.

Consequently

    S subset union_(j=1)^k H_j,     k<=N,     mu(H_j)<=beta M.

At least one cap has mass exactly beta M: otherwise the finite maximum of
the cap masses would be smaller, and the cover would bound every point's
depth strictly below beta. No assertion is made that these caps generate
all the facets of the exact Tukey region. In particular this result does not
contradict the vertical boundary-mass obstruction in
`candidate abe945997ae088f4`.

## 3. Fixing one separating cover constraint in each fiber

For each z put

    Q_z=intersection_j {x : (z,x) is strictly outside H_j}.

This is an open convex set, and K_z intersect Q_z is empty. If Q_z is empty,
there is no further constraint to impose at that fiber. Otherwise weak
separation of the compact convex K_z and the nonempty open convex Q_z gives
a nonzero b_z and a real c_z with

    K_z subset E_z={x:b_z.x<=c_z},
    Q_z subset {x:b_z.x>c_z}.

For clarity, strictness on Q_z follows from its openness: a nonconstant linear
functional cannot attain its minimum on a nonempty open set. One may take
c_z=sup_(x in K_z) b_z.x after orienting the separator as displayed.

Thus the ENTIRE fixed halfspace E_z is covered by the restrictions of the
H_j. Any new fiber K'_z contained in E_z remains covered by these same caps.
This is one linear support-function constraint per relevant integer fiber:

    h_(K'_z)(b_z) <= c_z.

It introduces neither a varying cap family nor a pointwise nonconvex cover
constraint on the new body.

## 4. An attained depth minimizer is an attained volume maximizer

Now suppose P is fixed and S_* is an attained minimizer of maximum normalized
halfspace depth among all positive-total-volume actual convex fiber families
with projection P. Existence in the nonhollow case is proved in
`candidate a14cc5f809b2b766`. Write its value as beta and its
mass as M_*. Construct the exact cap cover above and the fixed E_z at S_*.

Consider all actual compatible convex fiber families over this same P that
satisfy

    K'_z subset E_z                         whenever E_z was imposed,
    mu_(S')(H_j) <= beta M_*                for every j.

Then every such family has total mass at most M_*. Otherwise its fixed-cap
cover gives, for every candidate y in S', some containing H_j of mass at
most beta M_*, so

    maxdepth(S') <= beta M_*/mu(S') < beta,

contradicting the defining minimality of S_*. The original S_* satisfies all
constraints and attains mass M_*. Hence it is an actual GLOBAL maximizer of
volume for this fixed-cap, fixed-cover-support problem.

The normalization |K_(z_0)|=1 need not be imposed on competitors here: any
positive-volume family with this fixed nonhollow P has a positive central
fiber and can be rescaled into that normalization without changing its depth.
All competitors therefore belong to the same depth-minimization class.

The active mass constraints in this variational problem are precisely the
critical caps with mu_(S_*)(H_j)=beta M_*. Slack caps can be omitted from
first-order multipliers, although they remain part of the fixed covering
geometry. This result is a genuine optimization consequence of an attained
minimizer; it does not assume convexity or quasiconcavity of cap ratios under
Minkowski addition.

## 5. Positive-depth candidates are interior points of positive fibers

This geometric fact was supplied by the the contributor; here is the audited proof.
Let z in P and let F be the minimal face of conv(P) containing z, so z lies
in relint(F). Choose an exposing affine functional g on conv(P) with g=0 on
F and g<0 on P outside F.

If every fiber above F has zero d-volume, the vertical cap g>=0 contains
(z,x) and has mass zero. Otherwise the face body C_F has dimension
(dim F)+d. Positive barycentric weights at z within F imply that K_z has
positive d-volume. If x is on its boundary, (z,x) is a relative boundary
point of C_F. A nonzero supporting functional of C_F there has a nonzero
continuous component u: a purely integer supporting functional would be
constant on F because z is in relint(F), and hence zero on the relative
ambient space. Orient the supporting cap through (z,x) outward. On every
F fiber it intersects only a hyperplane with continuous normal u, and thus
has zero d-volume. Adding a sufficiently large positive multiple of g to
its integer component excludes all finitely many compact off-F fibers.
This gives an actual ambient closed cap of mass zero through (z,x).

Thus all zero-volume fibers and all boundaries of full-dimensional fibers
consist of depth-zero points. Conversely any interior point of a positive
fiber has positive depth: its fiber contains a small ball centered there,
and every containing halfspace contains at least half that ball.

Deleting zero-volume fibers preserves mu and the maximum depth exactly.
The positive-fiber index set P_+ is lattice-convex: if an integer z is a
convex combination of its points, the corresponding Minkowski combination
of positive fibers is full-dimensional and contained in K_z. The convex
hull of the positive fibers has precisely the same fibers at P_+ and no
other integer fibers. This is an exact support reduction. It does NOT by
itself transfer fixed-P minimizing optimality to all competitors over P_+.

## 6. Active continuous normals balance at each positive fiber maximum

For a fixed z and |u|=1 define the directional capacity

    c_z(u,t)=inf_a mu{(w,x): a.(w-z)+u.x>=t}.

The infimum is attained. Apply the affine-threshold compactification of
Section 1 to a minimizing sequence, observing that the threshold at z is
always exactly t. The realizing affine threshold retains that equality and
therefore has the displayed form for some finite a.

The function c_z is continuous on the unit sphere times R. Upper
semicontinuity follows by keeping an attaining a fixed and using zero
within-fiber boundary mass. For lower semicontinuity along (u_l,t_l)->(u,t),
choose attaining a_l and use the same threshold compactification. The finite
threshold at z now limits to t, so the realizing cap is admissible for the
limiting capacity. Its mass is the limit of the sequence of masses. This
gives the reverse semicontinuity inequality.

The unnormalized depth on fiber z is exactly

    D_z(x)=min_(|u|=1) c_z(u,u.x).

Vertical caps cannot give a smaller value. Indeed a vertical cap through z
can be replaced by a sufficiently strongly tilted nonvertical cap that
excludes its strictly excluded fibers, includes all its strictly included
fibers, and only cuts some boundary fibers. Its mass is no greater than the
vertical cap's mass. The finite saturation argument makes this replacement
with finite coefficients. Nonvertical containing caps can be moved inward
until their boundary passes through the candidate.

Let x_z maximize D_z on a positive fiber. The preceding section puts x_z in
its interior. Let U_z be its nonempty compact set of active unit continuous
normals, those satisfying c_z(u,u.x_z)=D_z(x_z). Then

    0 belongs to conv(U_z).

If not, choose v and eta>0 with u.v<=-eta on U_z. The inequality holds with
a smaller strict margin on a neighborhood of U_z. Since a ball of some
radius r about x_z lies in K_z, moving to x_z+t v decreases the cap threshold
in these directions by at least a constant times t and adds a within-fiber
slab of volume at least a fixed positive constant times t. This lower bound
holds for EVERY integer normal a, since its contribution vanishes on the
candidate fiber. All other fibers can only add mass under the same threshold
change. Thus all near-active directional capacities strictly increase.
On the compact complementary set of directions there is a uniform positive
gap above the maximum value, and continuity preserves that gap for small t.
This would strictly increase D_z, a contradiction.

Caratheodory now chooses at most d+1 active normals u_j and positive weights
lambda_j with sum lambda_j u_j=0. Choose their attaining integer normals.
The resulting ambient closed caps all pass through (z,x_z), have mass
D_z(x_z), and cover the ENTIRE continuous space above z: their margins there
are u_j.(x-x_z), whose positive weighted sum is zero, so they cannot all be
negative.

For a zero-volume fiber, the face argument in Section 5 supplies two
nonvertical zero-mass caps covering its entire fiber. Explicitly take an
exposer g=0 on its minimal face F with every F fiber of zero volume, a fixed
unit u, and the caps Tg(w)+u.x>=0 and Tg(w)-u.x>=0. For sufficiently large
finite T they exclude all original off-F fibers. At the chosen z they cover
all of R^d.

Therefore there is a finite critical cover with at most |P|(d+1) caps that
covers P x R^d itself, each of original mass at most beta M. All are actual
nonvertical ambient halfspaces. This cover has a larger cardinality than
Section 2 but a stronger geometric covering property.

## 7. The maximum-volume problem needs no extra cover constraints

Use the full-fiber critical cover of Section 6 at an attained fixed-P depth
minimizer S_*. Then S_* is a global maximizer of total mixed volume among
ALL compatible families over P satisfying only

    mu_(S')(H_j) <= beta M_*      for all fixed critical-cover caps.

Indeed the caps cover P x R^d regardless of the new fiber shapes, so the
same argument as Section 4 applies without any E_z constraints. The only
active budget constraints are caps of mass exactly beta M_*; all others
have strict slack. This is the coordinated fixed-cap variational problem
used in the next note's first-order stress equation.
